draft.title: What a logarithm is
card: A logarithm is an index. \(\log_{a}(x)\) is the index that \(a\) must be raised to, to give \(x\). The number \(a\) is called the base.
Example: \(2^{3} = 8\), so \(\log_{2} 8 = 3\). Read it as: 2 to what power gives 8? The answer is 3.
To work one out, ask the question in words. For \(\log_{3} 81\), ask: 3 to what power gives 81? Since \(3^{4} = 81\), \(\log_{3} 81 = 4\).
Logarithms undo indices. The statements \(a^{y} = x\) and \(\log_{a}(x) = y\) say the same thing. The first is index form and the second is logarithmic form, so you can swap between them.
draft.remember: A logarithm is a power: \(\log_{a}(x)\) asks what power of \(a\) gives \(x\).

a.why: \(5^{2} = 25\), so 5 must be raised to the power 2. The answer 5 is tempting because it is the base, but the logarithm is the power, not the base.

b.q: Which statement in index form is the same as the logarithm \(\log_{4} x = 3\)?
b.why: \(\log_{4} x = 3\) means 4 raised to the index 3 gives \(x\), so \(4^{3} = x\). The option \(3^{4} = x\) swaps the base and the index, which is a common mistake.
b.clue: The base of the logarithm stays the base of the power.
